588.t: Riverside albums, In the Red, Jamaica and Straight Ahead
588.s: She recounts That's Him, the early reputation as loony, the stage musical Jamaica, and writing Straight Ahead with Mal Waldron.
588.ch: New York and the Freedom Now years
588.q: Yes, the first album that I did with him was called "That's Him." He's the one who was A&R man, really. I made three albums for Riverside. He brought me to the jazz community, and then after "It's Magic," I think -- well, we had been performing the "Freedom Now Suite." We hadn't recorded it yet,…

588.t: Making the first album: Bob Russell and picking her songs
588.s: Bob Russell arranged for Benny Carter and Marty Paich; she chose the songs and built the album around a love story gone bad, though she was not yet writing.
588.q: That was Bob Russell who did that. It's always been for me like that. After Bob, it was Max and now there's Jean-Philippe Allard, somebody to help me to think because I don't know these musicians. I didn't know who Marty Page was or, I mean, I heard his name, but I wouldn't have thought to ask…

491.t: Stablemates' 14-bar structure; more artists record Golson's tunes
491.s: Golson and Brown discuss the unusual 14-bar form of Stablemates; Golson mentions Sonny Rollins and Lennie Niehaus recording his pieces.
491.ch: New York, Bostic and Dizzy Gillespie
491.q: Yeah, Sonny Rollins started recording. Everybody started recording. Incredible. This fellow that does all the music for Clint Eastwood. I can’t think of his name. He used to be an alto player. He wasn’t doing anything like that. He recorded my things. It was almost a dog. Called 411 West. He…

491.t: The Walkin' album: two orchestras in stereo
491.s: Golson only wrote for the Audio Fidelity album Walkin', conceived for stereo with a jazz orchestra on one channel and woodwinds on the other, but only one side was released.
491.q: Yeah. I didn’t play on that one. I just did the writing. That’s strange. That’s half of what that concept was, the way that turned out. Tom Wilson, who was the producer, joined Audio Fidelity Records. They were making records for a short while. He decided that since they’d embraced the stereo…

267.t: Head arrangements, Fats Domino and Bartholomew's collaboration
267.s: Ford explains how Bartholomew built records from head riffs, how the two split creativity with Fats, and how 'Blue Monday' went from Smiley Lewis to Fats.
267.q: He would say, I want this. Now if he had to sketch something out, he would, later on I believe he would sketch out a line. Me playing a baritone, I'd transpose, but a guy playing a piano would play the same thing. And that's how we did most of them, we'd write a line. Now later on, when I, with…

152.t: Java's credits and the RCA instrumental album
152.s: He explains the three-way credit with Toussaint and 'Friday', and that the songs were made up in the studio for producer Danny Kessler.
152.q: Well, not really. 33 and 3rd, big, uh, something like that because there's a guy by the name of some Friday that put his name on it.

278.s: Hercules was written for Aaron, recorded partly in Atlanta, and did little commercially.
278.ch: Later albums and the Neville connection
278.q: I think that was on the session in Atlanta, that we did some in Atlanta and some here. And a couple of Atlanta musicians, not a couple more than that of Atlanta musicians, like Barry Bailey, I think, who's with Atlanta Rhythm Section now.

878.t: Harry's own recordings: '339 March' and 'St. Louis Blues'
878.s: Harry says the Brownlee records were his only early recording, tells of '339 March', and the St. Louis Blues chorus with Wiggs, based on Larry's.
878.ch: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
878.q: Yeah, well, they, the manager of the band suggested that we would name it 339 March. So we recorded it on the Columbia record. Yeah. Called it 339 March. That's all the printout too.

571.s: They talk about Caledonia, played in a boogie style and recorded.
571.ch: Rockwell: Los Angeles club and sessions
571.q: it was a swinger you know that was the woody hermann number they would have the breaks and everything i think uh who sang that they do that break caledonia caledonia and then they just start swinging no it was really it was a boogie you know they had it in the boogie and it was yeah that was…

767.t: Oberstein records the reworked tune and Harris becomes Joe Harris
767.s: At the session the band plays the new version; Oberstein calls it an original, and Harris, asked for his name, takes the popular nickname Joe, so the record credits Joe Harris.
767.ch: Boots and His Buddies and Wild Cherry
767.q: He said, yeah man, but let him play what he's been playing today on this thing. We had no record on the music. We said, oh man, we've got some stocks here we've got to run over. Finally they got around to it. He said, let him play it man. Well they played it, the guy said, yeah man, that thing is…

803.t: The Jazz Speak album for Arbors Records
803.s: He explains how the Arbors album came after a Neal Hefti project, how he wrote tunes for Jeff Hamilton, John Clayton and Ted Rosenthal, and Rachel Domber's support.
803.q: Well that album was more the result of the musicians that I was working with. So I think I mean that’s going back five, six years now so I can’t remember the exact — I think what happened was I played with Jeff and John at the Vail Jazz Festival. I think we did a set together. And I mean I’ve grown…

898.t: 'Mr. Taylor' and Eric Reed's unison on the quartet recording
898.s: 'Mr. Taylor' was written for a friend and fan, not Cecil Taylor; Eric Reed chose to play the melody in unison, and Jackson speaks of standing out among countless recordings.
898.q: No. I know Cecil. It was written for a gentleman that I’ve known for quite some time, he’s a very, very good friend of mine and he’s just an avid jazz fan in general but he’s kind of my groupie, he’s followed me all over the world and I appreciate being around him. He’s got a great spirit about him…

563.s: He brought original tunes never rehearsed and the musicians made them work; they discuss risk of originals.
563.q: Oh yeah, I mean that’s another thing. In both cases on both of those albums, I brought in these songs and I had never heard them performed. We had no rehearsals as a band, just the guys are flying in front different places, or the guys just didn’t know each other or were too busy to get together to…

998.t: Making the CD and writing 'A Train' with Ray
998.s: Ray arranged everything with sidemen; he and Korb rework 'A Train' at the piano.
998.q: You know, Plas Johnson, Conte Candoli, Oscar Castro-Neves. It was just awesome. And I think out of that whole thing one of my favorite moments was when Ray, he came down to San Diego to my house, and we’re sitting at the piano going through some tunes and ideas, and we were going to do “A Train.”…

104.t: Her string CD of her own compositions
104.s: Recording her own tunes with Alan Broadbent's string arrangements after one rehearsal.
104.q: Well I played one or two — now I’ve made this, you may have heard this new CD with strings that I did a whole bunch of my own things. Finally I felt well I’d better do this before I lose my brain certainly — so I thought I’d better do it, so I did.

597.t: New record and the tune co-written with Rob Mounsey
597.s: Playing a tune from his new record, co-written with Rob Mounsey who wrote the bridge.
597.q: Yes. This is written by me and Rob Mounsey. Rob Mounsey is a great keyboard player and a great arranger/producer in New York. He’s done a lot of stuff. He’s done stuff for Sinead O’Connor, Madonna — he’s a brilliant, brilliant musician. I’ve played on two of his records. And this part he wrote.…

68.s: Tate recalls 'Ham and Eggs', 'Silver Chief' and how Lester Young wrote 'Tickle Toe' in Tulsa.
68.q: I like this — well I’ll tell you I like this song or recording date was called “Ham and Eggs” from the record you mean, you know like 78’s, they weren’t albums.

408.t: Stravinsky tone row in the Sun Suite and RCA freedom
408.s: Woods says a Stravinsky tone row sparked part of the suite and praises RCA's big budget and free rein.
408.q: I used the melody from the first [scats] that’s the tone row from one of Stravinsky’s early serial pieces. I used to know the name of it but I’m just blanking out. But I found the tone row anyway and that sparked that part of the piece.

223.t: The March 1954 Kenton sessions: Kingfish and Fearless Fosdick
223.s: Dick Lewis, the Four Freshmen, and the Kenton album of Holman and Russo originals, including the origin of Kingfish and a title changed for Capitol's lawyers.
223.q: Dick was the British Stan Kenton. He had a band too. Stan gave him a lot of charts. So he‟d recorded some of my things. Later on we got to be good friends. The Four Freshmen I don‟t know about.

503.t: Guitar Forms with Gil Evans, and records as Buzzy Bavarian
503.s: He explains how Guitar Forms came after Midnight Blue, with Creed Taylor and Gil Evans, and mentions his pseudonym.
503.ch: New York sessions, studio work and Midnight Blue
503.q: But I was struggling to maintain that, because there’s a bunch of albums between my first one and this one, but what I’m saying is that I felt if I hadn’t stopped all that other regular studio work my level would have started to go down. So an example of the level going up is the next album I’m…

220.t: The "Surprise! Surprise!" albums and the caricature cover
220.s: Wess untangles two albums with the same title and tells who drew the caricature cover, a guitarist from his ABC staff days.
220.q: Yeah, well, what happened was I had done a “Surprise! Surprise!” for a company in Oslow. I can’t think of the name of it right now. And then I did this other recording on a ship, on a cruise, actually it was. You know I was thinking that one had Frank Foster and Jimmy Heath. That was then and they…

371.t: 'Keeping Up with the Joneses' and Isham Jones
371.s: The Metro Jazz album of Thad and Isham Jones tunes was a marketing idea, likely Leonard Feather's; photo of the brothers.
371.q: I think Leonard Feather might have had a hand in that if I’m not mistaken. But, Isham Jones was a very popular songwriter at the time. He had written a lot of pop hits so they said, “Isham Jones, okay, that’s a Jones so let’s put him with Thad and so forth.” I see what they were doing from a…

225.t: The Total J.J. and J.J.! RCA albums for producer Jack Somer
225.s: Somer told Johnson to write everything and feature himself on the RCA big band albums.
225.q: He said, "J.J., on this recording project I would like for you to write all the material and to primarily feature yourself, so it's really J.J. Johnson’s baby." Da-da-da-dah. So I did sit down and write all these arrangements and whatever originals came out of that scenario.

165.t: Meeting King Pleasure and writing lyrics to Don't Get Scared
165.s: King Pleasure invited him to record Don't Get Scared and let him write his own words for the Lars Gullin solo.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: I met him when he – I was in the Turf bar at 52nd and Broadway. We all used to hang out in there, all the songwriters and performers. He came in. Somebody introduced me to him. I said, “Oh man.” I said, “You started me writing like that.” He says, “Yeah. That’s what I want to talk to you about.” I…

565.t: Who wrote Harlem River Drive and why it did not sell
565.s: Ronnie Cuber's role, composers' credits, and only the Weathermen buying it.
565.q: Hirscher and her husband then, Ira Hirscher (they’ve separated). David Hirscher and Ira Hirscher played with the Orquesta Broadway, the charanga, in the Palladium, and they were very talented. David Hirscher’s family owned the...another hotel in the Catskills, and I played there. I played Kutsher’s…

64.t: Mary Lou Williams's Cubano on the flutes album
64.s: He explains recording her piece Cubano after getting her to write out its bass line.
64.q: I don’t know if she recorded it but she used to play… Mary Lou and I worked opposite of one another on many occasions, at Downbeat, at the Composer and at several… at Café Society and even earlier then that. So every opportunity I got to be around her or to work opposite of her was a welcomed…

17.t: The Cozy Conception of Carmen LP
17.ch: Topsy aftermath, Africa and later career
17.q: Mine. And I loved all of those arias from the opera Carmen, and I just did it my way and put a little beat behind a lot of them you know, and start swinging those arias. Now I never tried to distort the melody, because there's too many opera lovers out there that love the melody of 'Carmen', so you…

90.t: Rappaport session titles and R.V.'s Wig
90.s: Titles from the session, and the record-selling fan R.V. who inspired 'R.V.'s Wig'.
90.q: Anyway, we did "Steady With Teddy" and "Bird Legs" and "Body And Soul" and "Roy's Boy," and Benny Bailey played a very beautiful solo all by himself on "Out Of Nowhere." All the compositions were mine, except "Out Of Nowhere" and "Body and Soul" and "Bird Legs," which was Benny Bailey's composition.

235.t: Hot Lips Page's St. James Infirmary date and his own tunes
235.s: Page recorded his tune La Danse for Columbia in 1947, and Deedle-ee Deedle-um was recorded with Timmy Rogers and later by Hendricks at Newport.
235.q: Well, "Lips" liked me and he said he wanted me, you know, to record with him. We rehearsed and we did it for Columbia and he recorded one of my tunes called "La Danse" and he let me play, you know, solos a and it was/beautiful, relaxed date, you know.

95.t: Naming her first songs and the session with Eddie Heywood
95.s: George urged her to name her songs, she called the first "Shorty George", and Eddie Haywood played the first session rather than George, adding his own tune.
95.q: (Unintelligible) recording, well, my brother George says, 'Let's name it.' So we did and that's when we named -- so I named the first song after him and I named it 'Shorty George.'

387.t: Memories of Goodman and Miller album
387.s: He reorchestrated little for the Sauter-Finegan album, done by mail from Germany.
387.q: It was all the same thing except reorchestrated. I could see no reason to change it because if I were to change it, why do that piece. So that's why it was that way. Also, it would be a lie to the title of the album.

125.t: Capitol recordings: April in Paris, and Stuffy as his first solo identification
125.s: Thompson recalls Capitol's Hollywood Stampede ballads and April in Paris, and Stuffy, born from group ideas with Hawkins, credited to the leader, and loved by Hawkins and Roy Eldridge.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: Particularly the ballads. I thought they were very good. We recorded "April in Paris", which was over recorded after that in many fashions, but it was later made famous by Bill Davis on the organ and Count Basie. One More Time.
